messages.content: Our conveyor keeps stalling at random times. What needs to be fixed?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the machine's fault record and the conditions around each stall. Safety floor: do not clear faults repeatedly to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact fault code, when it occurs (time of day, load condition), and what changed recently (belt tension, product type, ambient temperature), then re-ask with those in front of you.
The hydraulic system is acting strange. Pressure seems off sometimes. How do I fix this?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the machine's pressure log and the conditions around each event. Safety floor: do not bypass relief valves to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact pressure readings at idle and under full load, the time these events occur, and whether any changes happened to seals or pump settings, then re-ask with those details.
The diverter valve is not responding properly. What's the issue?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the valve's solenoid response log and the air supply conditions. Safety floor: do not apply manual force or jumper the solenoid, and no pressurized work. Next step: confirm whether it fails to shift, shifts slowly, or shifts but leaks; check inlet air pressure and check for moisture/debris in the lines; then re-ask with those observations.
The breaker is getting hot and trips sometimes. Is it bad?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the breaker's trip log and the circuit load profile. Safety floor: do not bypass or disable the breaker to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact current readings under normal and peak load, the number and timing of trips this week, whether the breaker is warm at idle, and if any wiring changes occurred, then re-ask with that data.
My pump isn't delivering like it used to. Flow is down. Can you tell me what's wrong?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the pump's discharge pressure and inlet conditions. Safety floor: do not bypass suction strainers or relief settings to force flow, and no energized work. Next step: measure inlet and discharge pressure, inspect the suction strainer for blockage, check the impeller for cavitation noise, and verify the inlet line for air leaks, then re-ask with those findings.
The indexer acts weird during fast runs. Keeps faulting. How do I get it to run stable?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the indexer's fault record keyed to the line speed and load. Safety floor: do not adjust speed limits or override faults to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact line speed when faults occur, the fault code (if any), cycle time, and whether the issue began after a parts change or setting adjustment, then re-ask with those specifics.
The fan is making noise and shaking more than before. What's going on?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the fan's bearing condition and balance state. Safety floor: do not run the fan with visible loose parts, and no energized work at height without fall protection. Next step: inspect the fan blades for damage or buildup, check all fasteners for tightness, measure vibration with your hand at the bearing (if safe), and note when the noise began relative to any recent maintenance, then re-ask with those observations.

asset: chain hoist in the maintenance bay

messages.content: The hoist brake isn't holding loads right. The load drifts down. Is it safe to use?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the brake's friction surface and spring tension. Safety floor: do not operate the hoist with a slipping brake or support a load by rope alone, and no energized work. Next step: inspect the brake lining for wear, contamination, or glazing; check the brake spring tension against the manual; measure the load drift rate; and verify when the drift started relative to last use or maintenance, then re-ask with that data.

asset: air compressor in the utility room

messages.content: My compressor keeps turning on and off really frequently. It's annoying. Why is it doing that?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the compressor's discharge pressure and the air demand load. Safety floor: do not remove or plug safety relief valves to stop cycling, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact tank pressure at which it cycles, measure the air usage rate during peak production, inspect the pressure switch set points and hysteresis, check for leaks downstream, and note if the cycling started after a demand change or setting adjustment, then re-ask with those findings.
The lift table hesitates partway up sometimes and groans. Sounds bad. What is it?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the table's hydraulic pressure profile and load curve. Safety floor: do not apply manual force or bypass relief valves to force motion, and no energized work. Next step: measure hydraulic pressure during the hesitation event, inspect the pump for noise and the cylinders for drift, verify the load weight when hesitation occurs, and confirm whether all four lift points are synchronized, then re-ask with those measurements.
The gearbox keeps losing oil. There's a slow leak somewhere. What do I do?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the seal condition and gear mesh integrity. Safety floor: do not operate with low oil level or bypass the breather to stop leaking, and no energized work. Next step: locate exactly where oil is dripping (drain plug, shaft seal, case joint, or breather), measure the leak rate per day, inspect the gearbox for damage or discoloration, check when the leak started relative to temperature changes or maintenance, then re-ask with that location and timeline.
The mixer keeps overloading and shutting down with some batches. I don't understand why.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the mixer's motor current trace and the recipe batch composition. Safety floor: do not disable the overload to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: identify which recipe batch triggers the overload (viscosity, density, or recipe change), measure motor current at startup and during mixing for that batch, check the blade condition for wear or damage, and verify the impeller clearances, then re-ask with that recipe specification and current data.
The motor current is running high. Is something wearing out?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the motor's load condition and mechanical resistance. Safety floor: do not reduce cooling or overload settings to suppress the reading, and no energized work. Next step: measure the exact current draw at idle, under normal load, and under peak load; verify supply voltage at the motor terminals; check for conveyor belt friction, seized bearing, or material carryback; and confirm when the high current began, then re-ask with those readings.
The valve takes too long to switch. Throughput is affected. What's the problem?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the solenoid coil response time and the air supply condition. Safety floor: do not increase pressure beyond rated or apply external force to speed the valve, and no pressurized work. Next step: measure the actual valve shift time in milliseconds, verify solenoid coil resistance and continuity, check inlet air pressure and desiccant cartridge condition, inspect for internal silt or corrosion, then re-ask with those electrical and pneumatic measurements.
The breaker keeps tripping even though the load shouldn't be that high. Why does this keep happening?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the actual load profile and the breaker's trip curve. Safety floor: do not disable or bypass the breaker to stop trips, and no energized work. Next step: measure the actual peak current during normal operation, verify the breaker's rated current and trip setting, check for harmonics or transient spikes with a power meter, inspect wiring for damage or corrosion, and document how many trips and at what load levels, then re-ask with that data.
The pump is making a grinding noise. Performance is getting worse. Is it failing?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the pump's inlet conditions and internal clearances. Safety floor: do not increase discharge pressure to force flow, and no energized work. Next step: verify inlet pressure (should not be below 0.2 bar absolute), inspect the suction strainer and inlet piping for blockage, check fluid level and condition, listen to pinpoint the noise (impeller or bearing), and measure the discharge pressure and flow, then re-ask with those findings.
The indexer stops sometimes for no reason I can see. Production line goes down. What should I check?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the indexer's fault history and the conditions when stops occur. Safety floor: do not bypass safety interlocks to force operation, and no energized work. Next step: capture the exact fault code when it stops (if any), the position where it stops most often, the time and line speed when stops occur, check for mechanical bind or jamming, and verify if stops correlate with temperature or shift changes, then re-ask with that timeline and error data.
Fan vibration keeps getting worse month after month. Is it just normal wear?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the fan's balance condition and bearing degradation trend. Safety floor: do not run with known mechanical imbalance or loose parts, and no energized work at height without fall protection. Next step: measure vibration amplitude (distance, velocity, or acceleration) now and compare to a month ago; inspect blades for corrosion, dents, or ice/dirt buildup; check bearing play and lubrication; and document the monthly trend line, then re-ask with those measurements.

asset: chain hoist in the maintenance bay

messages.content: The hoist drifts down, but not always. Sometimes it holds fine. This is inconsistent.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the brake's friction engagement and load history. Safety floor: do not operate a drifting hoist or rely on rope support alone, and no energized work. Next step: measure drift rate under different loads (half max, full max, overload); inspect brake linings for wear pattern (even vs. uneven); check load lever mechanism for play; document load type when drift occurs (smooth vs. jerky); then re-ask with those measurements and conditions.

asset: air compressor in the utility room

messages.content: The tank pressure gauge seems erratic. It jumps around. Is the gauge broken?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the gauge, the pressure switch response, or the tank's actual pressure stability. Safety floor: do not apply external pressure to test the gauge, and no energized work. Next step: verify the gauge reading against a known-good reference gauge; check the switch set points and hysteresis; inspect for water or oil in the air line (may cause gauge chatter); verify the tank pressure response to load changes; then re-ask with a direct comparison reading.
The lift table goes up tilted sometimes. Not level. How do I fix that?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the four-point synchronization of the lift cylinders. Safety floor: do not operate with tilted load or bypass relief valves to force balance, and no energized work. Next step: verify that all four cylinders raise and lower at the same speed under no load; measure the height at each corner during the tilt event; check hydraulic flow rates to each cylinder and the load sensor readings; inspect for internal cylinder drift or seal wear, then re-ask with those measurements.
The gearbox case gets warm and wet on the outside. There's moisture condensing. What does this mean?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the gearbox case temperature and the air dew point. Safety floor: do not operate in an explosion-proof area with temperature above rated limits, and no energized work. Next step: measure the case surface temperature, check the ambient air temperature and humidity, inspect the breather cartridge for blockage or saturation, verify the oil level and condition, and check whether condensation appears only during startup or during running, then re-ask with those thermal and hygric measurements.
The mixer torque varies a lot run to run. Sometimes high, sometimes normal. Same recipe each time.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the batch composition variability and the mixer's mechanical condition. Safety floor: do not bypass torque limits to run high-variability batches, and no energized work. Next step: verify batch starting temperature, ingredient density, and moisture content are truly identical; check blade clearances for wear; measure drive motor current and torque sensor output across 10 runs; inspect gear mesh for wear patterns; then re-ask with that ingredient and mechanical data.
The motor current keeps slowly increasing over the past few weeks. It's trending up. What's happening?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the conveyor's mechanical resistance and the motor's thermal aging. Safety floor: do not reduce ventilation or raise temperature limits to suppress symptoms, and no energized work. Next step: compare current readings at the same load over time; check conveyor belt tension and alignment; inspect rollers for wear and bearing noise; verify supply voltage is stable; measure motor winding temperature; and confirm whether the current rise correlates with ambient temperature or runtime, then re-ask with that trend and mechanical data.
The valve seems to be leaking internally. I can hear a hiss. Is it done for?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the valve's spool seals and the seat contact. Safety floor: do not operate a leaking valve beyond the manufacturer's rated leakage, and no pressurized work. Next step: measure the actual internal leakage rate (bubble test or flow meter); listen to identify whether the leak is from inlet to exhaust or pilot drain; inspect the valve for external damage; check air quality and desiccant condition; verify when the leak started relative to maintenance or pressure spikes, then re-ask with that leakage data and timeline.
Every time I run the full production load the breaker trips. It's been getting worse lately.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the actual load current under full production and the breaker's trip threshold. Safety floor: do not bypass or disable the breaker to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: measure the peak current when the breaker trips; verify the breaker's calibrated trip current; check for load changes or added equipment since the problem started; inspect wiring and connections for resistance or heating; measure load harmonics with a power analyzer, then re-ask with the actual trip current and load equipment list.
The discharge pressure keeps fluctuating up and down. It's not stable.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the pump's flow stability and the system's pressure control. Safety floor: do not increase pressure set points to force stability, and no energized work. Next step: measure the exact pressure oscillation frequency and amplitude; check for cavitation or air in the suction line; verify the relief valve cracking pressure and hysteresis; inspect for clogged discharge filter or downstream restrictions; and confirm whether oscillation occurs at all flows or only at specific operating points, then re-ask with those pressure traces and flow conditions.
The indexer isn't stopping at the same position every cycle. Placement is off. What's worn out?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the indexer's encoder accuracy and the mechanical backlash. Safety floor: do not disable position checking to force operation, and no energized work. Next step: measure the position error across 20 cycles; verify the encoder output and signal quality; check gear backlash and bearing play; inspect for load variation between cycles; confirm whether drift is consistent or random; and verify if drift started after a parts replacement or shock load, then re-ask with those measurements and maintenance history.
The fan is making a weird squealing noise we never heard before. Something is different.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the fan bearing condition and the acoustic signature change. Safety floor: do not run with a noisy bearing or loose parts, and no energized work at height without fall protection. Next step: compare the current noise to a recording from before the change started; check bearing temperature with an infrared thermometer; inspect for grease dryness or contamination; measure vibration at the bearing housing; verify whether the noise is present at startup, during running, or both, then re-ask with those observations and a timeline of when it began.

asset: chain hoist in the maintenance bay

messages.content: The hoist doesn't lower smoothly all the time. Sometimes it's jerky. Sometimes fine.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the brake friction consistency and the control valve settings. Safety floor: do not force smooth lowering by bypassing the brake, and no energized work. Next step: lower a full load and measure descent speed and jerkiness (video record and measure time); inspect the brake friction surface for glazing, wear, or contamination; check the brake spring tension; verify the control valve spool condition for stiction; and document load weight and type when jerkiness occurs, then re-ask with those observations and load specifications.

asset: air compressor in the utility room

messages.content: The discharge air coming out of the compressor is hot. Much hotter than it should be. Is it broken?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the compressor's internal temperature and cooling system performance. Safety floor: do not reduce cooling air flow or disable temperature monitoring, and no energized work. Next step: measure discharge air temperature and compare to the compressor manual specification; verify inlet air temperature and filter condition; check the cooler core for blockage; measure compressor load and duty cycle; verify if high temperature correlates with high ambient or extended runtime, then re-ask with those temperature measurements and ambient conditions.
The lift speed isn't consistent. Sometimes it goes up fast, sometimes slow. Same button push.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the hydraulic flow path and pressure regulation. Safety floor: do not increase pump pressure to force consistent speed, and no energized work. Next step: measure lift time over 10 cycles without load; measure lift time under rated load; measure pump discharge pressure and flow rate; check solenoid valve response time and proportional valve linearity; inspect cylinders for internal drift; and verify whether speed variation correlates with temperature, then re-ask with those timing and hydraulic measurements.
The gearbox is grinding. Loud noise from the gear mesh. It's getting worse.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the gear tooth contact and internal wear pattern. Safety floor: do not operate a grinding gearbox without shutdown limits, and no energized work. Next step: verify oil level and condition (check for metallic particles or sludge); measure the grinding frequency against the shaft speed to confirm it's the mesh; inspect the oil strainer and magnetic plugs for wear debris; verify alignment and mesh backlash; check when grinding started relative to oil changes or load increases, then re-ask with those forensic findings.
When the mixer starts, the current spikes really high for a moment. Is that normal?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the motor inrush transient and the loaded blade mechanics at startup. Safety floor: do not reduce soft-start ramp time to suppress the spike, and no energized work. Next step: measure the startup current spike amplitude and duration; compare to the motor's inrush specification; verify the blade isn't mechanically locked before start; check the load inertia against the motor rating; measure the actual batch viscosity and temperature at startup; then re-ask with those electrical and mechanical conditions.
The motor feels hot to the touch all the time now. I'm worried about the insulation.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the motor winding temperature and thermal resistance. Safety floor: do not override thermal protection or reduce cooling to let insulation age faster, and no energized work. Next step: measure the winding temperature (via bearing thermometer if infrared won't work); compare to nameplate thermal class; check if motor cooling air is unrestricted; measure ambient temperature; verify the load current matches nameplate rating; perform an insulation resistance test (megohm reading); then re-ask with those thermal and electrical measurements.
The valve is sluggish to respond. Shift is slow. Did the solenoid fail?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the spool seals and the solenoid force balance. Safety floor: do not apply manual force to move the spool, and no pressurized work. Next step: verify solenoid coil continuity and resistance; measure voltage and current at the coil terminals during actuation; inspect the solenoid air gap; check for silt or corrosion on the spool bore; verify inlet air quality and pressure; measure the actual shift time in milliseconds, then re-ask with those electrical and pneumatic findings.
The breaker is acting flaky. Sometimes the circuit drops for a moment then comes back. Power isn't stable.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the breaker contacts and the mechanism latching. Safety floor: do not bump or tap the breaker to force closure, and no energized work. Next step: document the exact time intervals and duration of drop-outs; measure circuit voltage and current during and between drop-outs; inspect the breaker mechanism for wear and play; check incoming service voltage stability; verify whether drop-outs correlate with temperature, vibration, or load changes, then re-ask with those electrical traces and environmental notes.
The pump seal is starting to leak a little. There's dripping at the base. Can I keep running it?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the seal wear rate and the product compatibility. Safety floor: do not run beyond the manufacturer's rated leakage without floor containment, and no energized work. Next step: measure the leak rate (drops per minute); check seal temperature; verify the pump has appropriate bearing coolant or flush plan for the product type; inspect the impeller and shaft for wear grooves; determine when the leak started and whether any seal maintenance or temperature changes occurred, then re-ask with that leak rate and timeline.
After many cycles the position error keeps adding up. End of shift it's way off. What accumulates?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the encoder calibration and the servo loop accuracy. Safety floor: do not disable position checking or use hardware limits to force operation, and no energized work. Next step: zero the indexer and capture position every 10 cycles for 100 cycles; plot the cumulative error trend; verify encoder resolution and mounting integrity; check the servo tuning parameters (gains and settling time); inspect for mechanical hysteresis or drag, then re-ask with that error trend and servo settings.
The fan vibrates more when the weather changes. Hot days are worse. Is the bearing expanding?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the fan's aerodynamic surge and thermal stress effects. Safety floor: do not run with known imbalance or loose components, and no energized work at height. Next step: measure vibration amplitude at different ambient temperatures (hot, cool, humid); check clearances between blade and shroud in hot and cool conditions; inspect bearing radial and axial play; verify the blade pitch or angle hasn't changed; check the air path for blockage that changes with temperature, then re-ask with those vibration and thermal trend measurements.

asset: chain hoist in the maintenance bay

messages.content: The hoist lowers in a jerky stop-and-go pattern. It's not smooth at all.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the brake engagement dynamics and the control valve stiction. Safety floor: do not force smooth descent by disabling brake control, and no energized work. Next step: lower a full load and record the descent (measure time-position profile); inspect the brake disk friction surfaces for glazing or wear bands; check the brake spring tension; measure control valve spool resistance across its travel; verify the load weight and whether jerkiness is load-dependent, then re-ask with that descent profile and mechanical inspection data.

asset: air compressor in the utility room

messages.content: The discharge air has oil mist in it. I can see it in downstream equipment. Where is it coming from?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the compressor's oil separator and the air outlet design. Safety floor: do not run above rated discharge temperature or without the separator element, and no energized work. Next step: verify the oil level is not overfilled; check the separator element for tears or bypass; measure discharge pressure and compare to rated maximum; inspect the mist eliminator if one exists; verify drainage paths are unblocked; determine whether carryover started after maintenance or temperature rise, then re-ask with those separator and thermal findings.
One corner of the lift table drifts down when it's supposed to be held. The others are fine.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in that cylinder's seal condition and internal leakage. Safety floor: do not apply manual wedges or bypass the holding valve, and no energized work. Next step: measure how fast that one corner drifts (inches per minute); compare the cylinder pressure between corners under load; perform a cylinder rod-pull test to check for internal seal wear; inspect the holding valve for that circuit; verify the load sensor for that corner, then re-ask with those hydraulic and seal-integrity measurements.
The gearbox seal surface looks rough and pitted. Will it still hold?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the seal mating surface texture and the sealing pressure dynamics. Safety floor: do not operate without proper seal material or with known damage, and no energized work. Next step: measure the pit depth with a precision tool; check the seal material (elastomer condition); verify the counter-face finish; test for leakage under full load; determine if pitting is passive (corrosion) or active (fretting); compare to the seal manufacturer's surface finish spec, then re-ask with those material and leakage measurements.
Product is sticking to the blade and shroud. It builds up between batches. How do I stop this?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the product's adhesion properties and the mixer's clearances. Safety floor: do not run with heavy product buildup (can unbalance the blade), and no energized work. Next step: inspect the blade-to-shroud clearance geometry; verify the product viscosity and temperature at discharge; measure carryback mass per cycle and trend it; check the blade design against the product viscosity class; determine if carryback started after a product change or blade replacement, then re-ask with those clearance measurements and product specs.
Sometimes the motor runs away briefly before the VFD catches it. Is the motor failing?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the motor's electromechanical transient and the VFD control loop response. Safety floor: do not disable VFD protection or mechanical braking to test the motor, and no energized work. Next step: capture the VFD current and speed trace during runaway events; measure the runaway duration and peak speed; verify the VFD tuning parameters (proportional and integral gains); check for load inertia changes; inspect mechanical braking function; determine whether runaway correlates with load changes or ambient temperature, then re-ask with those drive traces and control settings.
The exhaust from the valve is getting restricted. Backpressure is building up. What's blocking it?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the muffler element condition and the downstream restriction. Safety floor: do not remove or bypass the muffler without proper venting, and no pressurized work. Next step: measure exhaust backpressure; compare to manufacturer specification; disassemble and inspect the muffler element (porous insert condition); check downstream air lines and silencers for blockage; verify whether blockage developed gradually or suddenly; then re-ask with those pressure and blockage-location findings.
The breaker won't hold load anymore. It just keeps tripping at full load. The contacts must be worn.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the contact erosion pattern and the actual trip current. Safety floor: do not disable the breaker or bypass it to keep running, and no energized work. Next step: measure the trip current with the breaker under full load; inspect the contacts visually for erosion patterns; verify the breaker's rated current and compare to the load; test the breaker on a known-good circuit to confirm if the trip is device-specific; document when the problem started relative to maintenance or high-inrush events, then re-ask with those contact photos and trip current data.
The pump output pressure keeps dropping slowly over time. The flow seems weak. Is something eroding inside?

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the pump's internal geometry change and the product erosivity. Safety floor: do not run at elevated pressure to compensate, and no energized work. Next step: measure discharge pressure trend over the past week; compare current pump curve (pressure vs flow) to the original spec sheet; check for debris in the discharge line; inspect the inlet for product contamination or corrosive agents; verify operating hours since last impeller replacement; then re-ask with that pressure trend and inspection findings.
The indexer complains about load sometimes. Gets an error. But the product weight is correct.

That description alone cannot isolate a cause, and I will not guess one — it lives in the inertia profile and the servo response. Safety floor: do not disable load checking or override faults to force operation, and no energized work. Next step: verify the actual product mass and inertia match the indexer's calibration; measure acceleration time to index velocity; check for mechanical binding or friction that varies; inspect the servo loop tuning parameters; confirm whether load errors correlate with specific products or line speeds; determine when calibration last occurred, then re-ask with those mass and acceleration measurements.
